segments.text: MAXWELL ZEFF: Well, so we're very
lucky to have this group here.
A lot of the people here are responsible for the way AI
looks today in the real world.
And everyone here is also working
on how it should look in the next couple of years.
So I think this is a wonderful opportunity
to have this discussion.
We're not going to shy away from the hard questions.
So I guess the first one is, maybe just to start high level,
do we have the right architecture
to get to this next level of AI?
Do we have-- are transformers the right thing
to get to RSI, continuous learning?
I think I want to start with Jerry on this one.
Let's start here.
JERRY TWOREK: OK, it's a spicy one.
But I feel like I'm being asked a lot about it.
My theory of AI research is that you always
should try to think what is the bottleneck of the day.
What is the thing-- why are today's models not 10 times
better than they are right now?
And while doing what we've been doing and keeping investing
in transformers, building new environments,
scaling up training gives us gains--
those gains are predictable, we already know how to do it--
I think architecture is the biggest thing that
can give us gains beyond those things
that we already know how to do.
I genuinely believe-- and record this,
remember-- that the next two years will
be like the time of architecture,
where the biggest gains and the biggest
progress in the deep learning will
come from trying to step away from the transformers.
We have been like--
the discovery of transformer has been an inflection point
for AI research.
Scaling transformers and doing pre-training
has been another moment where the age of scaling has started.
But transformer has carried us very far.
And I think it is kind of like a little bit like holding us
back right now, where I believe for the same cost,
you probably can train much better agent
with a different architecture.
We just don't know that architecture yet,
and it's a time to find it.
That's what I think.
MAXWELL ZEFF: Oriol, you guys are working a lot
on, as you just said, RSI.
Do you think transformers are the right thing to get us there?
ORIOL VINYALS: Well, first of all,
I guess transformers have transformed over the years.
So if you look at the actual model today,
it resembles, but it's not the same.
So every iteration of a new model we see outside, especially
the ones you can also see in the open source,
I mean, there's a lot of tweaks in the architecture already
happening.
So definitely, there's a hill climbing.
Perhaps to Jerry's point is a bit
of a local optimum around the transformer.
But that's very important.
I'm not sure I would believe that I want--
I mean, is there a better transformer-like thing
that is much more efficient?
Possibly.
I feel like when I think of architecture,
I think holistically, not just the brains,
but also the whole agent that you build around it.
That architecture, I feel, has a lot of more low-hanging fruits
to optimize, like its memory system, how it
compresses context, and so on.
So I would probably bet on disruption
there first, although I'll be rooting for, obviously,
better architectures that I'm sure they'll
publish in NeurIPS 2027 or so.
MAXWELL ZEFF: No comment there, I guess.
Dawn, I'm curious for your thoughts on this.
DAWN SONG: Oh, yes.
This is a very good question.
I was talking to Jerry earlier.
The question is, which will go faster?
Yes, I think potentially there ought
to be some other architecture there
that will be more effective than transformers.
The question is, how far-- so we have two paths.
The one is we continue down the current path with transformers.
And then I think a number of people
here are working on RSI and so on.
So then, with RSI, as even with the current path,
the AI can continue to improve.
And then with RSI, then it can help potentially
to find better architectures.
Then that's one path.
And another path is we have humans.
We have experts like Jerry to try to discover,
design new architectures.
And the question is, which path will get us sooner there,
especially given that--
I think we can also do a poll here for people to think--
what everyone here thinks about the timeline.
When are we getting to RSI with this path?
And I'm actually very curious to hear.
MAXWELL ZEFF: OK, well, let's do a poll.
So who thinks we're going to get to RSI this year in 2026?
Zero.
OK.
Hands go up or down.
We can't do--
OK.
OK.
WEIZHU CHEN: Sort of.
MAXWELL ZEFF: Any hands?
Maybe you need to say the year.
What year do you think RSI is coming?
DAN ROTH: So I'm not going to make a prediction because I
think this is not necessarily the key question when
you ask about whether the technology is
ready for something.
So we are in an agentic summit here.
And why do we move to agents?
I mean, one reason we move to agent is the-- really,
an admission by model providers and everyone that we cannot
think about just models.
We need to think about systems.
And so when we think about systems,
today, we are still coupling an agent with a model.
But that's going to change.
I mean, so we're going to decouple agents for models.
And the architecture is going to change also the model level.
But the system level is the one that I think is more important,
because people realize that we have to be able to delegate,
we have to use solvers, we have to use expert models, and so on.
And to me, the key differences are
going to happen at that level.
And over time, transformers also are going to change.
So transformers is a very recent beast.
There's no reason that in 10 years,
this is going to be the component that we rely on.
But still, the question that are around
how to build intelligent systems with solvers,
with expert system and so on, that's
going to stay even when we change the underlying
architecture of the model itself.
DAWN SONG: Yeah, I have some questions of-- for that, too.
I think this is also another question for debate, is, one,
how much of the power or the differentiation
is at the model level versus actually at the agent level?
And also-- so we have been doing some work.
I think others have been doing this work as well.
So as the model becomes smarter and smarter--
so right now, when people build agents,
there is still a lot of human design.
Yes, we talk about memory systems, compaction,
and all these different things.
You still have humans, designers.
But as the model gets smarter, the model essentially
can build agents themselves.
So we actually recently developed
an open framework, agentic framework.
We call it AI-centric agent development framework, where
we have the model to actually build agent itself on the fly
and build all these different components and so on.
As the model gets smarter and smarter,
it actually can do this very well.
So then there is-- it also begs the question then going forward
whether we actually still need to build these--
yeah, here we are at the Agentic AI Summit.
But there is a question whether-- even next year,
what are we going to do?
Are we just going to have model to actually write
the entire agentic system framework and so on?
MAXWELL ZEFF: Wojciech, I'm curious for your thoughts
on that.
WOJCIECH ZAREMBA: So few things.
So there's a question about what's
the mental model for the AI development?
And you might think that maybe AI development
is like stacking up a LEGO piece after piece that is actually not
even that hard to make an improvements in the,
let's say, the memory piece or having architectures
more efficient.
It's just like you keep on stacking it up,
and models become better and better.
Or alternatively, you might be thinking
that actually doing AI research is similar to developing
relativity theory.
You need this-- like a genius, like a massive brain to come
up--
so far, historically, we have seen that primarily we
are in the world number one.
There has been few instances of these breakthroughs,
like a transformer, as people mentioned.
But still, we can keep on hill climbing, building
LEGO piece one after another.
And it seems that the models might reach the,
you can call it, escape velocity.
So in some sense, they can be good enough such
that they can continue stacking up the LEGO pieces.
So you build the model that gets 150 IQ, then you get 200 IQ,
Of course, there is a question about the asymptote,
if that would continue.
And it might be the case that if it continues for sufficiently
a long period of time, it's like if it keeps on improving, then
even if there are some necessary breakthroughs needed,
then the good enough model might crack them.
So now, whether or not the escape velocity
would be achieved, whether or not
there is enough energy put into the system, that's the question.
Or when would that happen?
MAXWELL ZEFF: Weizhu, I'm curious for your thoughts
on this kind of system versus the core architecture
kind of debate.
WEIZHU CHEN: Yes, I think for the RSI,
basically, it highly depends on just,
like, say, the system, including this kind of the higher
environment, the evaluation, which kind of task
you want to solve.
I think from the model point of view,
as long as you are able to specify the task very clearly--
but I think this is pretty challenging.
It's the most difficult part.
And it's easier for the model for the-- if the RSI is trying
to--
OK, specific to this task, it's doable in the next two or three
years.
But if you want to say, OK, if it's need to be very generic,
I think it's much, much harder, maybe 100x harder.
So there's a huge difference.
Yeah.
From the architecture point of view, I think, in my opinion,
it's about architecture, finally, is still
defined by the model capacity, how many parameters
you have in the architecture.
And yeah.
So nothing is for free for the architecture,
definitely not free lunch.
When you get something good, it's
going to sacrifice the other part for a lot of case.
Yeah.
MAXWELL ZEFF: Yeah.
I think, just to move the conversation along a little bit
with our time, I'm curious-- also,
there's been this incident recently
in the last couple weeks of-- it's
really brought to light how much security and safety is so
important with agents nowadays.
We might not have RSI today, but agents are very capable.
We've seen OpenAI's agent, hack Hugging Face.
Anthropic said its agents have escaped containment, too.
Maybe-- Dawn, I'm curious for your thoughts
based on your security background.
I'm curious what you think, how these incidents
shifted your thinking about safety and security with agents.
DAWN SONG: OK, great.
Yeah, thank you.
Thanks for your question.
And so, first, I actually want to clarify some things.
So first of all, actually, in the OpenAI's case,
what the agent was trying to do, it
was tasked to actually solve tasks
in the benchmark ExploitGym, which is what we developed.
And there have been various blogs written about it.
I want to take the opportunity to clarify a few things.
So first of all, that ExploitGym,
the OpenAI deployed ExploitGym in
their internal infrastructure.
And so that's their internal deployment.
And also, so what the agent did was-- somehow
the agent figured out, oh, maybe in order to solve the tasks,
maybe Hugging Face has some data or information related to this.
So it went to--
decided to go to Hugging Face to try to find this.
And then, actually, before this incident became publicly known,
we actually got an email from Hugging Face asking us, oh,
there's-- so we also developed another benchmark, CyberGym.
So CyberGym and ExploitGym, they actually covered
the entire-- the lifecycle for vulnerability, vulnerability
discovery and then exploit generation.
So we actually got an email from Hugging Face asking,
oh, there's CyberGym, like essentially serving points.
And they seem to have some vulnerabilities, like asking us,
do you guys know this?
And then we looked into this.
We said, oh, actually, this is not our CyberGym.
MAXWELL ZEFF: [LAUGHS]
DAWN SONG: So basically, some third party
deployed some service on Hugging Face.
And they also called this CyberGym.
I think they copied probably some things
from the CyberGym benchmark, but they called it CyberGym.
And then, in the end, that's actually
what the agent was able to exploit through that
and then got into Hugging Face inference and so on.
So I wanted to clarify that.
Even though that one was called the CyberGym,
but, actually, it's entirely a third-party deployment.
It has nothing to do with us.
So we actually clarified with Hugging Face for their blog
and so on.
But anyway, so this, I think, is a wake-up call.
Even though-- my group, so we have been among the earliest
to actually investigate in this space,
looking at impact of frontier AI in the landscape
of cybersecurity.
And we did all this work.
Also, I was trying to essentially
raise the awareness earlier for the community to get prepared
and to take action, because I could
see even-- we started working in this space actually two
years ago.
Even then, I could see with the AI fast progress
and so on, this is what's coming.
Although, actually, I have to say,
even though we built out this benchmark and demonstrate it,
I was trying to talk to people even in the policy space,
that we need to get prepared.
But I think it was difficult for people
to really understand and get the message.
So I think what happened was the Mythos certainly helped.
And also, I think this incident really
is a wake-up call for people that the agents' capabilities
now have reached a level.
DAN ROTH: So I want to say that it's clearly a wake-up call.
But I think we shouldn't think that this is only
the cybersecurity problem.
This can happen everywhere.
So we saw earlier today the Tetris example.
But imagine that you have a multi-agent system
and the agents communicate among themselves,
and you impose some constraints on what information
they can communicate to each other.
So Dawn doesn't want some of the information
that the agent has about her to be communicated
with Max's agents or my agent.
Now, we can put a verifier that verifies
that they don't break these kind of rules
of what can be communicated.
But the agents can go around it and maybe change the language
that they're using so that the verifier is
incapable of verifying what they're doing.
So this issue goes much beyond just cybersecurity.
It goes to any communication system that involves agents.
And we have to really think about it
from basis, what are the issues that we have to deal with?
And I think we are a little bit dormant in this space.
DAWN SONG: Yes, absolutely.
I think, yes, the risk is vast, covers a broad range.
And I think in cyber, in particular,
I think just given that already, we
know there's huge incentives for attackers to attack.
And now, really with frontier, it significantly
reduced their, essentially, cost and also the expertise level
that's needed and so on.
So this can really bring a huge sea change in the space.
MAXWELL ZEFF: Wojciech, from a resilience perspective,
what do you think?
WOJCIECH ZAREMBA: So I was thinking,
what's the mental model of what's happening now?
And maybe one mental--
so OK.
It doesn't seem that what just happened
is like a last incident, OK?
That doesn't seem so, OK?
Quite opposite, it seems that we are entering a new era, OK?
So maybe one way to think about it
is imagine what happens if all the sudden locks to the houses
stop working.
You can just enter every house.
What happens?
So that's what-- that's the era that we are
entering with cybersecurity.
We should expect in the very close future
that the open-source models will become insanely good in cyber,
and that will be a problem.
That will be a problem for critical infrastructure.
It will be a problem both from perspective of teenagers hacking
for fun, people who are motivated to hack for the gains,
and also nation states.
And all of these will be at play.
My guess is that it will be chaotic.
MAXWELL ZEFF: Any other thoughts from the panel here?
JERRY TWOREK: I think cybersecurity is one angle.
Definitely, we probably already live in a world
where we are lucky that OpenAI and Anthropic are good guys,
but they probably can hack any company in the world
if they want to, which is a scary realization.
But there's other angle from a perspective of reinforcement
learning researcher which I am a bit worried,
which is misalignment and reward hacking, which we have seen
there and escaping the sandbox.
And that's something that everyone
who works on reinforcement learning I
would like them to be really, really care about and really,
really worry about, because in some ways,
we are training those models to get reward
in various environments, in various situations.
And it's up to us, the researchers, the trainers,
the people building that systems what is actually rewarded.
And whenever we are building an environment where the model can
hack, where the model can do unethical things,
the model can do incorrect things to get reward,
the model will do it.
The model will learn it.
The model will express that behavior in the real world.
And we are putting more and more of our life
in the hands of the models, and we'll
be only doing more and more.
AI is great, and everyone is using it.
And the reward-hacking models, if they
are exposed to the real world, they
will be doing things that are not great,
and they are trained for that by us.
So designing your environments in a way that
promotes the right types of behaviors
and the right types of taking actions
is what really everyone should be doing.
And I think there almost should be like some standards.
You don't get to train your models
if you don't build your environments carefully
enough because we don't want to be having
misaligned models everywhere that
are trying to exploit whatever sandbox they
are in to get their reward.
It's a really, really scary thing to think about.
MAXWELL ZEFF: Well, on that note, we are out of time.
But thank you to the panelists for a great conversation.
If we give a round of applause for the panelists.
And thank you so much, everyone.
Appreciate it.
[APPLAUSE]
